title: Antepartum foundations
intro: Follow conception through prenatal assessment. Sort normal maternal changes from findings that need urgent evaluation.
number: GTPAL: count pregnancies separately from births. Twins count as one pregnancy and one delivery in their gestational-age category, but two living children if both survive.
contrast: Gravida includes the current pregnancy. For an uncomplicated twin birth at term with both children living and no other pregnancies, G1 T1 P0 A0 L2.
recall: A missed period is a symptom; fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound is direct evidence.

title: Nutrition, labor and fetal monitoring
intro: Read a contraction and its fetal heart-rate response together. Connect nutrition and pain relief to maternal and fetal assessment.
number: Contraction frequency runs from the start of one contraction to the start of the next. Duration runs from the beginning to the end of one contraction.
contrast: A baseline fetal heart rate of 110–160 beats/min is generally expected. Always interpret the baseline with variability and decelerations.
recall: Early decelerations mirror contractions. Variable dips suggest cord compression. Late dips follow the contraction peak and can signal impaired placental exchange.

title: Pregnancy and birth complications
intro: Work from the bleeding pattern, the blood pressure or the delivery cue to the priority action. Include obstetric emergencies and surgical birth.
number: Blood pressure at or above 160 systolic or 110 diastolic in pregnancy is severe range. Notify the team promptly and confirm according to the urgent pathway.
contrast: Painless bleeding raises concern for previa; painful bleeding with a tender uterus suggests abruption. Either needs urgent assessment. Avoid digital vaginal examination until previa is excluded.
recall: McRoberts flexes the maternal hips. Suprapubic pressure is applied above the pubic bone by a trained team member. Fundal pressure can worsen shoulder impaction.

title: Postpartum and newborn care
intro: Assess uterine tone and bleeding, recognize postpartum complications, and connect newborn feeding, warmth and breathing to nursing care.
number: Check the Apgar score at 1 and 5 minutes. A newborn who needs ventilation needs immediate support; care begins before the score is completed.
contrast: A boggy uterus suggests atony. Persistent bright bleeding with a firm uterus points toward trauma. Escalate heavy bleeding in either case.
recall: A wet infant loses heat by evaporation. A cold scale causes conduction. A draft causes convection. A cold nearby window causes radiation.

title: Maternal–newborn comprehensive final
intro: The course final covers the official content for Modules 1–13. Revisit the four unit exams from reproductive planning through the high-risk newborn.
number: Tie each assessment to its time point: prenatal screening, stages of labor, minutes after birth, then postpartum recovery.
contrast: At birth, distinguish maternal bleeding from newborn breathing needs. Both patients may need simultaneous assessment and help.
recall: Trace the route from pregnancy to labor to postpartum. At each point ask whose status changed, what threatens perfusion or breathing, and how to check the response.

title: Pediatric assessment and development
intro: Choose communication, pain assessment, play and safety teaching that fit the child's developmental stage.
number: FLACC has five behaviors scored 0–2 each, for a total of 0–10. Follow the change after an intervention.
contrast: Use serial growth measurements and a developmentally appropriate chart. A trend is more informative than a single percentile.
recall: Parallel play fits toddlers; cooperative rule-based play becomes more prominent in school-age children. Match teaching to what the child can understand.

title: Blood disorders, immunity and pediatric neuro
intro: Connect pallor, bleeding, fever, rash or a change in behavior to the blood cell, immune process or neurologic function involved.
number: Time a seizure from onset. A convulsive seizure reaching 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery, needs an emergency response.
contrast: Compare behavior and responsiveness to the child's baseline. An infant may show irritability or a bulging fontanelle rather than an adult pattern.
recall: Red cells carry oxygen, platelets help stop bleeding and neutrophils fight infection. Decide which function is failing before choosing a precaution.

title: Pediatric breathing and circulation
intro: Listen to where the sound comes from and look at how hard the child is working. Connect cyanosis, feeding fatigue and poor perfusion to the cardiac problem.
number: A peak-flow plan compares today's value with the child's personal best. The usual green zone is at least 80%, yellow 50–79% and red below 50%.
contrast: A quiet chest in a tiring child with severe asthma can signal very poor airflow. Reassess work of breathing and alertness immediately.
recall: Stridor points toward the upper airway. Wheeze often reflects narrowed lower airways. A blue spell in tetralogy of Fallot suggests reduced lung blood flow.

title: Musculoskeletal, endocrine and GI disorders
intro: Use pain pattern, hydration and breathing to tell an expected finding from a threat to the limb, the circulation or the bowel.
number: For a weighed diaper, about 1 gram gained equals 1 mL of urine. Use measured output and the child's weight to follow hydration.
contrast: Pain out of proportion under a cast, especially with passive stretch, can precede loss of a pulse.
recall: In a telescoping bowel, pain can surge and then ease. A quiet interval does not rule out an urgent problem.

title: Pediatric comprehensive final
intro: Renal and genitourinary disorders are the new content. The final also revisits development, blood and immune disorders, neuro, breathing, circulation, endocrine, GI and mobility.
number: For weight-based medication calculations use kilograms. Convert pounds to kilograms by dividing by 2.2; check the prescribed dose against the safe range and maximum.
contrast: Follow urine output, daily weight, blood pressure and edema together when kidney function changes.
recall: Distinguish nephrotic protein loss from nephritic inflammation. Use the earlier exams to rehearse airway priorities and age-appropriate assessment.

title: Eye, ear, infection and immunity
intro: Distinguish urgent loss of vision, modes of transmission and rapidly worsening allergic reactions.
number: For a visual-acuity result such as 20/40, the first number is the testing distance. The second describes what a person with standard vision can read at that distance.
contrast: A normal-looking eye does not exclude retinal detachment when new flashes and a curtain-like field loss are reported.
recall: Separate a local rash from systemic allergy: airway symptoms, breathing difficulty or poor perfusion change the urgency.

title: Burns, endocrine disorders and diabetes
intro: Check airway risk in burns, then use urine, sodium, glucose and mental status to distinguish endocrine and diabetes emergencies.
number: Typical adult serum sodium reference range is 135–145 mEq/L. DI tends toward high sodium with dilute urine. SIADH tends toward low sodium with concentrated urine.
contrast: For an awake adult able to swallow with glucose below 70 mg/dL, the usual 15–15 rule is 15 g of fast carbohydrate and a glucose recheck in 15 minutes. Typical fasting glucose is 70–99 mg/dL.
recall: Clear lungs do not clear a burn airway. Likewise, a glucose number alone does not distinguish DKA from HHS: look for ketones, acidosis, dehydration and mental-status change.

title: Neurologic change, stroke and spinal cord injury
intro: Start with time of onset and neurologic baseline. Compare movement, level of consciousness, swallowing and breathing before choosing the priority.
number: Glasgow Coma Scale: eyes 1–4, verbal 1–5 and motor 1–6. Report individual components and the trend, and document any untestable component.
contrast: With suspected acute stroke, last known well is the last time the patient was at neurologic baseline, even if the deficit was first noticed later.
recall: A sudden severe BP rise after spinal cord injury suggests autonomic dysreflexia. Lower pressure in neurogenic shock is a different pattern.

title: Reproductive disorders and disaster nursing
intro: Separate postoperative outflow problems from expected drainage, then practice the change from one-patient emergency care to mass casualty triage.
number: During bladder irrigation, urine output = total drainage minus irrigant infused over the same interval. For 1,850 mL drained and 1,500 mL infused, urine output is 350 mL.
contrast: For adult START, red means immediate, yellow delayed, green minor and black deceased or expectant according to the applicable criteria. Reassess after initial sorting.
recall: A green or yellow tag can change if the person's breathing, perfusion or mental status worsens.

title: Adult health comprehensive final
intro: Shock and multiple organ dysfunction are the new content. Revisit each earlier exam using one question: is tissue perfusion, ventilation or neurologic function getting worse?
number: For adults with septic shock on vasopressors, an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg is common. Assess mentation, urine output, skin perfusion and trends alongside pressure.
contrast: Match the mechanism: volume loss empties the tank, cardiogenic shock weakens the pump, distributive shock changes vascular tone and obstructive shock blocks forward flow.
recall: Compare response with the patient's own baseline. A transiently improved pressure alone does not prove adequate organ perfusion.
